questions.stem: What is Model Deployment in Machine Learning, and how does it make a trained model available for real-world predictions?
options: Model Deployment means saving training results on a developer's computer where the model can be tested again. A separate prediction interface is unnecessary for real-world use.
Model Deployment is complete when a model achieves high validation accuracy, because that proves it can answer requests from users without any production service or integration.
Model Deployment moves training data into a production server so the model can continue fitting after each user request. Predictions are returned only after that fitting step.
Model Deployment is the process of making a trained Machine Learning model available in a production environment. It allows applications or users to send input data and receive predictions.

questions.stem: What are the main steps involved in deploying a trained Machine Learning model from development to production?
options: Deployment begins by making the model publicly reachable, then collecting its dependencies and environment settings from runtime errors. Testing is postponed until production requests have accumulated.
Model Deployment involves saving the trained model, preparing its dependencies, creating a prediction interface, testing the system, and releasing it to a production environment.
Deployment mainly involves exporting model weights and uploading them to storage. The serving interface, input validation and runtime dependencies can be reconstructed automatically by users.

Deployment requires retraining the model on live inputs after release, then choosing a suitable software environment. Saving its trained state and testing request handling are optional preparation steps.

questions.stem: What is the difference between real-time inference and batch inference, and when is each deployment approach used?
options: Real-time inference means collecting requests continuously but calculating predictions at fixed intervals. Batch inference handles each request immediately so callers receive responses without waiting.
Real-time inference is chosen when models run on GPUs, while batch inference is selected when the same model uses CPUs. The difference depends on hardware rather than request timing.
Real-time inference generates predictions immediately when requests arrive. Batch inference processes groups of inputs at scheduled times or in bulk without requiring immediate responses.
Real-time inference serves results using only previously stored predictions; batch inference runs the model each time an individual user submits a new request, avoiding any scheduling.

questions.stem: How do REST APIs, containers, and cloud infrastructure work together to serve Machine Learning models in production?
options: REST APIs receive prediction requests and return model outputs. Containers package the model and its dependencies, while cloud infrastructure provides computing resources to run and scale the service.
REST APIs package model dependencies inside an isolated image, containers supply public request endpoints, and cloud services mainly provide the format used to serialize prediction inputs.

REST APIs receive requests and return predictions, but containers by themselves automatically increase computing capacity for every traffic spike without requiring deployment orchestration or cloud resources.
REST APIs route requests to a model, while containers install the model's training dataset from scratch on each request. Cloud infrastructure replaces the need for runtime dependency management.

questions.stem: Why are model versioning, dependency management, and reproducible environments important for reliable Model Deployment?
options: Model versioning tracks model files, but dependencies should be updated to the newest releases whenever production starts. Reproducible environments matter only for retraining, not serving.

Model versioning identifies which model is live, while dependency management is unnecessary once it passes local tests. A rollback can restore previous predictions without restoring previous software.

Reproducibility requires saving the trained weights alone, because containers and package versions do not affect output behavior. Versioning is useful only when creating a completely different architecture.
Model versioning tracks deployed models and supports rollback. Dependency management and reproducible environments keep software versions and configurations consistent, reducing deployment failures.

questions.stem: How do Canary Deployment, Blue-Green Deployment, and Shadow Deployment reduce risks when releasing updated Machine Learning models?
options: Canary Deployment routes copied requests to a new model without using its predictions, Blue-Green Deployment gradually raises its traffic share, and Shadow Deployment switches all users at once.

Canary Deployment exposes a new model to limited traffic, while Blue-Green Deployment switches between separate production environments. Shadow Deployment tests a new model using copied traffic without affecting live predictions.
Canary Deployment sends all live traffic to a new version after testing, Blue-Green Deployment compares predictions silently on mirrored requests, and Shadow Deployment serves a limited user share.
Canary Deployment and Blue-Green Deployment both require replacing the current model in place with no fallback, while Shadow Deployment gives users the new model's outputs immediately.

questions.stem: How can deployed Machine Learning models be monitored and optimized for prediction latency, throughput, scalability, data drift, and model performance degradation?
options: Deployment monitoring can focus on average accuracy alone because good prediction quality automatically implies low latency and adequate throughput. Autoscaling addresses every type of drift.
Latency and throughput can be optimized by running additional predictions for each request. Data drift should be treated as a request-volume problem instead of a change in feature distributions.

Production monitoring tracks response time, request volume, resource usage, data drift, and prediction quality. Autoscaling, inference optimization, alerts, and model retraining help maintain reliable performance.
Monitoring can track latency and traffic while using recent predictions as labels to retrain automatically. Retraining before independent evaluation prevents performance loss after every data shift.
